_about.what: Machine-readable description of the COSMOS XMP library (XMSG from PLANC), for a linter.
_about.library: ND-10609 COSMOS Programmers Library, XMP module, version B02 (02.06.86).
sources: Installation/Software/ND-10609/files/XMP-B02-IMPT.readable.txt - the routine and type declarations (AUTHORITATIVE for signatures)
Installation/Software/ND-10609/files/XMP-B02-DEFS.readable.txt - the library-layer constants (AUTHORITATIVE for XMOK and the XMX... standard values)
SINTRAN/XMSG/SINTRAN-CHAT/XMSG-PL-VALUES-L.INCL - the release-L constants off D100 (AUTHORITATIVE for the raw MON 200B layer)
Reference-Manuals/ND-60.164.3 EN COSMOS Programmer Guide.md - the per-routine reference (parameter NAMES and purposes)

_about.companion: PLANC-XMSG-API-RULES.md - the checkable rules for a linter author.
_about.include_rule: Include XMP-B02:DEFS + XMP-B02:IMPT for library work, OR XMSG-PL-VALUES-L for raw MON 200B work - NEVER both. They share 184 constant names and a redeclaration in PLANC is fatal, not a warning.

XMUSERADDRESS.note: TYPE XMUSERADDRESS = INTEGER for the ND-100/ND-500 and the NEW MC68000 compiler. The file's own comment: the OLD MC68000 compiler, whose default INTEGER is INTEGER2, needs INTEGER4. Build one with ADDR(buf(0)) FORCE XMUSERADDRESS - ROUND brackets; the guide prints square ones and PLANC F rejects them.

flags.summary: Every XF... option constant is a BIT POSITION, not a value. Write 2**XFWTF, never 15.

XFWAK.note: 0x4000 - oracle-confirmed on the wire in this repo

flags.flags_is_always_first: Every routine except the XMPB* buffer builders takes flags as parameter 1. Where no option is defined, pass 0.
flags.many_bits_share_a_position: Bit 13 is XFPON, XFUSG, XFHIP, XFRRO and XFEXC depending on the call; bit 12 is XFOPS, XFRES, XFRMR and XFBNC; bit 10 is XFROU and XFRDI. The meaning comes from WHICH ROUTINE you pass it to.

error_model.summary: The XMPF* library does NOT return the kernel's negative XE... numbers. It returns POSITIVE 'STANDARD values' rebased on XKXXX. XMP-B02:DEFS states it: 'the STANDARD value symbols are the normal XMSG symbols prefixed by XM-'.

not_terminated.meaning: EXACTLY the base value, and it is NOT an error. It means 'not terminated' - for a receive with flags 0 it means THE PORT IS EMPTY.

success.note: The raw MON 200B kernel's OK is 1; the library remaps it to 0.

xrout_base.note: XROUT errors also travel on the WIRE, in byte 1 of a return message, as the small positive XR... number - NOT rebased. Two representations, one meaning.

error_model.buffer_routines: The XMPB* buffer-formatting routines answer -1 on a bad buffer, which is not a symbolic status at all. Test them separately.
error_model.receive_exception: A receive (xmpfrcv / xmpfrre / xmpfrrh) is the one call whose success is not only XMOK: the raw kernel returns the MESSAGE TYPE (XMTNO=1..XMTPS=6) as a successful status. Accept XMOK OR XMTNO..XMTPS. Do NOT test '> 0' (that accepts XMXENTM=16896 and every error) and do NOT test 'if status = 0 only' unless you have measured that your kernel/library pair always remaps.

xmpopnm.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpopnm.purpose: Open a port and give it a name in XROUT. A plain named port - it has NO free-connection counter.
xmpopnm.notes: Sends a message to XROUT, so it CHANGES the task's 'task current' message. The opened port becomes the task's default port. A name longer than XMMAXNameLength returns -1. If another open port already holds the name, an error status comes back.

xmpclnm.purpose: Close a port and clear its name in XROUT.
xmpclnm.notes: The counterpart of xmpopnm / xmpopcn. Note SINTRAN also closes a task's ports when the task terminates - measured on D100 2026-08-20.

params.name: maxConnections

xmpopcn.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpopcn.purpose: Open a NAMED CONNECTION port with a seat count. XROUT keeps a free-connection counter for it.
xmpopcn.notes: Guide: 'When somebody contacts portName by sending a letter via XROUT, XROUT looks at the free connection counter and if it is greater than zero, XROUT decrements it and forwards the letter. If there are no free connections, XROUT tries to find another port with the same name.' So a seat is spent by XROUT BEFORE the server sees the letter. Only the port's owner puts one back, with xmpinfc. Like xmpopnm this changes the 'task current' message and makes the port the task's default port.

params.name: extraConn

params.name: serialNumber

xmpinfc.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpinfc.purpose: Give a seat back to (or take one from) a connection port's free-connection counter.
xmpinfc.notes: DOES NOT WAIT for XROUT. The reply arrives LATER as a message on portNumber, so a receive loop must expect it. Changes the 'task current' message and the 'port current' message on portNumber. If the resulting free count would go negative, XROUT returns an error.

xmpread.notes: Same as xmpfrea but names the message explicitly.

xmpwrte.purpose: Write user data into a SPECIFIED message buffer (not necessarily the current one).
xmpwrte.notes: Options: XFRES (bit 12) resets the message length to 0 before writing.

params.name: localPort
params.note: The sending port - where XROUT's reply will arrive.

xmprout.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmprout.purpose: Send a message to, or via, the local routing task XROUT. This is the call that looks a destination up BY NAME.
xmprout.notes: The message must already carry an XROUT header (build one with xmpbini/xmpbast/xmpbrdy, or an XSLET letter header with xmpblet). Sending an XSLET letter to a remote CONNECTION port SPENDS ONE SEAT on that port - XROUT decrements the free-connection counter to forward it. If the name is unknown, or the connection port has no free seats, XROUT returns the message to the sending port with an error status, and the caller sees it as a message rather than as a bad returnStatus.

params.name: flags
params.note: 2**XFSEC for a secure send, 2**XFHIP for high priority, 2**XFFWD to forward.

params.name: remoteMagicNum

xmpsend.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpsend.purpose: Send a SPECIFIED message to another task, by magic number.
xmpsend.notes: Guide: 'The message specified by msgIdentifier is set as task current message and as port current message for localPort. Then the message will be sent as described under XMPFSND.' Prefer this over xmpfsnd whenever the program called xmpfget itself: xmpfget makes the new buffer TASK current only, and xmpfsnd would pick the PORT current message if one exists. MEASURED on D100 2026-08-18: xmpsend to a port whose task had died returned XMOK - it does NOT validate the destination. Set 2**XFSEC to learn about undeliverable messages; they come back as a message of type XMTRE.

xmpfopn.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpfopn.purpose: Open an UNNAMED port. Nobody can look it up by name; you reach it by magic number.
xmpfopn.notes: The opened port becomes the task's default port; when it closes, the previously opened port becomes the default again.

xmpfget.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpfget.notes: The new buffer becomes the TASK current message. It does NOT become the port current message - there is no port parameter - which is why a program that builds its own reply should send with xmpsend rather than xmpfsnd. Every buffer you get must eventually be released (xmpfrel) or sent (xmpfsnd / xmpsend / xmprout / xmpfrtn).

xmpfrel.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpfrel.purpose: Release a message buffer back to XMSG.
xmpfrel.notes: Release a received message once you have read it out; a buffer you neither send nor release is leaked message space (XMXEMFL is what a leak eventually looks like).

params.name: flags
params.note: 2**XFWTF waits; 2**XFWAK arms a general wake-up; 2**XFHIP means 'wake up on status change if no high-priority message is waiting'.

params.name: startScanPort
params.note: Where to start the scan.

params.name: portNumber

xmpfgst.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpfgst.purpose: General status: scan ALL of the task's ports and report one that has a message waiting.
xmpfgst.notes: Guide: 'A task may have many open ports. It does not always know on which one the next message is arriving. XMPFGST allows the task to check all ports belonging to the task.' THIS - not xmpfrcv - is the call that looks at more than one port. It only NAMES the port; you still have to call xmpfrcv on the port it returns. UNVERIFIED on real hardware in this repo: no program here has yet used xmpfgst; the working two-port server polls each port with xmpfrcv and flags 0 instead.

xmpfrea.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpfrea.purpose: Read user data out of the TASK CURRENT message into your own buffer.
xmpfrea.notes: Takes NO message identifier - it acts on the task current message, which is what the last successful receive or xmpfget made current. The length that arrives from the wire is the SENDER's choice; PLANC checks no array bounds, so passing it straight in lets a peer write past the end of your array.

params.name: flags
params.note: 2**XFRES (bit 12) resets the message length to 0 first.

xmpfwri.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpfwri.purpose: Write user data from your buffer into the TASK CURRENT message.
xmpfwri.notes: Takes NO message identifier, same as xmpfrea.

xmpfrhd.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpfrhd.purpose: Read only the 6-byte header of a message buffer.

xmpfwhd.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpfwhd.purpose: Write the 6-byte header of the TASK CURRENT message.
xmpfwhd.notes: Note it takes no message identifier - unlike xmpwrhd.

params.name: flags
params.note: 2**XFSEC secure, 2**XFHIP high priority, 2**XFBNC bounce, 2**XFFWD forward, 2**XFROU send to XROUT.

xmpfsnd.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpfsnd.purpose: Send the CURRENT message to another task, by magic number.
xmpfsnd.notes: Guide: 'the current (default) message buffer is assumed, namely the port current message if one exists, or, if none, the task current message.' That two-step choice is the trap: after a receive there may still be a port current message, and xmpfsnd will send THAT rather than the buffer you just built with xmpfget. Use xmpsend when you built the buffer yourself.

xmpfrtn.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpfrtn.purpose: Return a message to the port it came from, writing word 0 first.
xmpfrtn.notes: The cheap way to answer a request without needing the sender's magic number.

params.name: flags
params.note: 0 = return at once. 2**XFWTF = block until a message arrives. 2**XFWAK = arm a wake-up on this port. Flags are BIT POSITIONS.

params.name: localPort
params.note: The ONE port to receive on. 0 means the task's default port.

params.name: msgType
params.note: XMTNO / XMROU / XMTHI / XMTRE / XMKIK / XMTPS.

params.name: remotePort

params.name: msgLengthOrStat

xmpfrcv.returns: INTEGER status. On a SUCCESSFUL receive the library returns XMOK (0) with the type in the msgType out-parameter; the raw kernel returns the message type itself (XMTNO..XMTPS), and both forms have been seen, so accept either. An EMPTY port answers XMXENTM (16896).
xmpfrcv.purpose: Receive a message queued on ONE named port.
xmpfrcv.notes: THERE IS NO RECEIVE-ON-ANY-PORT. One call, one port (ND-60.134.2 section 4.3.2.10). A successful receive makes the message TASK current, and PORT current too if it was sent secure. With flags 0 an empty port answers XMXENTM (16896). With 2**XFWAK a wake-up bit is armed on the port: 'When the wake up is done, the message is not received, and so the receiving must be repeated' - a doorbell, not a delivery. The wake-up can be armed on more than one port at a time, but that does NOT make one call watch two ports: MEASURED on D100 2026-08-21, a two-port server armed on both parked on the admin port while a message sat on the room port.

params.name: flags
params.note: 2**XFWTF wait, 2**XFWAK wake-up, 2**XFRMR (bit 12) release the message if the last byte is read.

params.name: userLength
params.note: CLAMP - this is your buffer's size, not the sender's.

xmpfrre.purpose: Receive on ONE port and read the message into your buffer in one call.
xmpfrre.notes: Same one-port rule as xmpfrcv. Safer for buffer length than the receive-then-read pair, because userLength is YOUR number rather than the sender's.

params.name: bytes0To1OrStat
params.note: Normally the first 2 bytes of the message; if msgType is XMTRE, the error status.

xmpfrrh.purpose: Receive on ONE port and read the first two bytes of the message.
xmpfrrh.notes: Identical to xmpfrcv except it gives the first two data bytes instead of the length.

params.name: flags
params.note: 2**XFWAK arms a wake-up; 2**XFHIP means 'wake up on status change if no high-priority message is waiting'.

params.name: queueLength
params.note: Number of messages queued for localPort.

xmpfpst.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpfpst.purpose: Look at ONE port to see whether a message is waiting - without receiving it.
xmpfpst.notes: Does not unchain the message. The queue length is one instant's answer and is stale as soon as it is read.

params.name: remoteMagicNum

xmpfmst.returns: INTEGER status returned as the PLANC out-value: 'name(...) =: returnStatus'.
xmpfmst.purpose: Get a received message's status - and, above all, the sender's FULL magic number.
xmpfmst.notes: xmpfrcv only hands back a HASHED port, which cannot be used to answer. xmpfmst is how a server gets an address it can send to. It OVERWRITES the length variable, so keep the receive's own msgLengthOrStat first if you still need it (on an XMTRE it was the reason for return, not a length).

xmpblet.notes: It only prepares bytes in your own buffer - it copies nothing into an XMSG message and sends nothing. You then xmpfget a buffer, xmpfwri the header in, xmpfwri your own data AFTER it, and xmprout it. Returns -1 if headerBuffer is not even-aligned or lengthBuffer is too small.
